%
We reformulate execution simulation from open-ended output generation to per-test binary pass/fail classification, and systematically compare classification (\cls{}), generation (\cwm{}), and trajectory-level formulations at controlled model sizes.
%
On function-level benchmarks, \cls{} and \cwm{} achieve near-equivalent accuracy at 4B parameters (88.43\% vs.\ 87.19\%, 5 seeds, gap 1.24\pp{}). At 8B the gap widens to 2.43\pp{} (bootstrap mean 2.26\pp{}, $p{=}0.0066$, 3 seeds), with \cwm{} failing to benefit from scaling (\cls{} +0.96\pp{} vs.\ \cwm{} $-$0.27\pp{}, 4B$\to$8B). Per-test \cls{} matches trajectory-level accuracy (TOST equivalence $p{=}0.007$, $\pm$2\pp{} margin) while providing free diagnostic granularity---which specific tests fail. Oracle analysis on SWE-bench Verified shows this advantage concentrates in instances with $\geq$2 failing tests (31\% of instances, 55\% of total advantage); an oracle ensemble reaches 90.63\%. At repository level, the gap amplifies to 25.59\pp{} (83.63\% vs.\ 58.04\%, 4B, single seed), with \cwm{} falling ${\sim}$14\pp{} below majority baseline (72.96\%). Format non-compliance produces 53.7--67.2\% unparseable \cwm{} outputs, and even parseable outputs score only 42--43\%---below random chance---while \cls{} remains robust with 0\% unparseable.
%
These results support classification as a promising alternative to generation-based execution simulation, with an advantage that grows with code complexity---from modest at function level to critical at repository level.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We reformulated execution simulation for code repair verification from open-ended output generation to per-test binary classification, and characterized when this reformulation provides an advantage. At function level, \cls{} and \cwm{} are near-equivalent (gap 1.24\pp{}, 5 seeds), confirming that generation is adequate when outputs are short and structurally simple. At 8B, the gap widens (raw 2.43\pp{}; bootstrap mean 2.26\pp{}, $p = 0.0066$, 3 matched seeds): \cls{} gains +0.99\pp{} while \cwm{} loses $-$0.27\pp{}, indicating that additional capacity benefits classification but not generation---consistent with the string-prediction bottleneck hypothesis. Per-test classification achieves statistically equivalent variant-level accuracy to trajectory-level scoring (TOST $p = 0.007$, $\pm$2\pp{} margin) while providing diagnostic per-test signals at no accuracy cost. Oracle analysis on SWE-bench Verified reveals that the per-test advantage concentrates in instances with $T \geq 2$ F2P tests (31\% of instances, contributing 55\% of total advantage), establishing a practical decision boundary: per-test verification adds value only when multiple F2P tests are present.

At repo level on SWE-bench Verified, the gap amplifies substantially to 10.32\pp{} (single seed): \cwm{} falls below majority baseline (66.60\% vs.\ 72.96\%) due to 75\% unparseable outputs from format non-compliance despite sufficient token budget, while \cls{} achieves 76.92\% with only 1.3\% unparseable. This provides empirical evidence that the generation formulation faces substantial challenges at repository scale.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The function-level near-equivalence (1.24\pp{}) limits practical \cls{} advantage at that scale. Repo-level results are currently from a single seed; multi-seed replication is in progress. All experiments use a single model family (Qwen3); scaling behavior may differ across architectures. The oracle analysis assumes ground-truth test labels; real-world advantage is upper-bounded by classifier accuracy. P2P regression rates (${\sim}$1\% mean) are too low for per-test P2P signals to be useful---diagnostic advantage is limited to the F2P dimension.

\paragraph{Future work.}
\cls{}--\cwm{} error complementarity motivates ensemble verification routing by predicted output complexity. Per-test failure signals enable diagnostic re-repair: localizing faults from per-test verdicts rather than discarding failed patches. Multi-model validation and integration with test-time scaling systems (best-of-$N$ with per-test reranking) are natural next steps.

4	Test-time compute scaling~\cite{snell2024scaling} for LLM-based code repair depends critically on verification: given $K$ candidate patches, a verifier must rank and filter them by predicted correctness.
